In an inverted chord , the lowest tone is not its root ; an inverted melody is one in which its intervals are inverted. An interval is inverted by raising or lowering either of the notes using displacement of the octave (or octaves) so that both retain their names (pitch class). For example, the inversion of an interval consisting of a C with an E above it is an E with a C above it - to work this out, the C may be moved up, the E may be lowered, or both may be moved. Under inversion , perfect intervals remain perfect, major intervals become minor and the reverse, augmented intervals become diminished and the reverse.
